paragraphs: Democracy does not attach men strongly to one another, but it puts their everyday dealings on an easier footing. Suppose two Englishmen happen to meet at the Antipodes, surrounded by strangers whose language and manners they hardly know. At first they will stare at each other with great curiosity and a kind of secret uneasiness. Then they will turn away, or, if one speaks to the other, they will take care to talk only about very unimportant subjects, in a constrained and absent manner. Yet there is no enmity between these men; they have never seen each other before, and each believes the other to be respectable. Why, then, do they keep so warily apart? We must go back to England to learn the reason.

When birth alone, regardless of wealth, determines men’s classes in society, everyone knows exactly where he stands on the social scale. He does not try to rise, and he does not fear falling. In a community organized this way, men of different castes have very little contact with one another. But if chance brings them together, they are ready to talk without hoping or fearing to lose their own position. Their relations are not on a footing of equality, but they are not strained. When an aristocracy of money replaces an aristocracy of birth, things change. The privileges of some are still very great, but the chance of acquiring them is open to all. It follows that those who hold privileges are constantly haunted by the fear of losing them or of having others share them. Those who do not yet enjoy them long to possess them at any cost, or, failing that, at least to appear to possess them, which is not impossible. Since men’s social importance is no longer openly and permanently fixed by blood, and varies endlessly with wealth, ranks still exist, but it is not easy to tell at a glance who belongs to which. Secret hostilities then arise in the community. One set of men tries by countless devices to get in among those above them, or to seem to. Another set is constantly up in arms against these usurpers of their rights. Or rather, the same individual does both at once: while he tries to rise into a higher circle, he is always on the defensive against intrusion from those below him.

Such is the condition of England today, and I believe the peculiarity I mentioned above is chiefly due to it. Aristocratic pride is still very great among the English, and the boundaries of the aristocracy are poorly defined. So everyone lives in constant dread that someone will take advantage of his familiarity. Unable to judge at once the social position of the people he meets, an Englishman prudently avoids all contact with them. Men fear that some slight service they render may draw them into an unsuitable acquaintance. They dread civilities, and they avoid a stranger’s intrusive gratitude just as much as his hatred. Many people put these odd anti-social tendencies, and the reserved, taciturn bearing of the English, down to purely physical causes. I may grant that there is something of this in their race, but much more is due to their social condition, as the contrast with the Americans proves.

In America, privileges of birth have never existed, and wealth gives its owners no special rights. There, men who do not know each other readily frequent the same places and find neither danger nor advantage in freely exchanging their thoughts. If they meet by chance, they neither seek nor avoid conversation. Their manner is therefore natural, frank, and open. It is easy to see that they hardly expect or fear anything from each other, and that they care no more to display than to hide their position in the world. If their demeanor is often cold and serious, it is never haughty or constrained. If they do not talk, it is because they are not in the mood, not because they think it in their interest to keep silent. In a foreign country, two Americans are at once friends, simply because they are Americans. No prejudice repels them; their common country draws them together. For two Englishmen, the same blood is not enough; the same rank must bring them together. The Americans notice this unsociable mood of the English as much as the French do, and are no less astonished by it. Yet the Americans are tied to England by their origin, their religion, their language, and partly by their manners; they differ only in social condition. It may therefore be inferred that the reserve of the English comes much more from the constitution of their country than from that of its inhabitants.
